items.prose: A limit order fills with chance $p$ and then costs $-h$ against the mid. A miss costs $h + c$.
items.question: Write $E[\text{limit}]$ with the bracket expanded and like terms collected.

feedback.correct: $E[\text{limit}] = h + c - 2p\,h - p\,c = h + c - p(2h + c)$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Write $-p\,h + (1 - p)(h + c)$, then expand the bracket.

byKey.no-miss-h: You dropped the $h$ from the miss cost. The bracket is $(1 - p)(h + c)$.
byKey.sign: You left out the $p$ terms. Expand $(1 - p)(h + c)$ and add $-p\,h$.

explain.text: $-p\,h + (1 - p)(h + c) = -p\,h + h + c - p\,h - p\,c = h + c - 2p\,h - p\,c$. Each extra point of fill chance cuts the cost by $2h + c$.

items.prose: Add adverse selection to the model. A filled bid tends to fill just before the price falls. Measured a minute later, a fill costs $-h + a$, not $-h$. A miss still costs $h + c$, and a market order costs $h$.
items.question: Put the lines in order to find when the limit is cheaper.

lines.text: $p(a - h) + (1 - p)(h + c) < h$, the limit must cost less than the market order
$p\,a - p\,h + h + c - p\,h - p\,c < h$, expand the brackets
$c < p\,(2h + c - a)$, take $h$ from both sides and move the $p$ terms right
$p > \dfrac{c}{2h + c - a}$, divide by $2h + c - a$, positive when $a < 2h + c$

feedback.correct: $p > c/(2h + c - a)$: adverse selection raises the bar.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Start from the comparison, expand, collect the $p$ terms, then divide.

explain.text: With $h = 2$, $c = 1$ and $a = 2$ the threshold rises from $1/5$ to $1/(4 + 1 - 2) = 1/3$. If $a \geq 2h + c$, no fill chance makes the limit worth it.

items.title: Executing a large order
items.prompt:
A fund must buy 60,000 shares of a mid-cap today. Best bid £19.98, mid £20.00. The asks hold 10,000 shares at £20.02, 15,000 at £20.03, 20,000 at £20.05 and 25,000 at £20.08.

(a) Find the average price and the cost against the mid of one market order for all 60,000 now.

(b) Find the cost if the fund sends six market orders of 10,000 through the day and the book refills to the same prices each time. State what this assumes.

(c) Instead it posts six limit bids of 10,000 at £19.98. Each fills with chance 0.6; a miss means buying 10,000 at £20.03. Find the expected cost against the mid, and the best and worst cases.

(d) Recommend a plan, and name two reasons the numbers in (b) and (c) may be too optimistic.
items.model:
**(a) One market order.** It walks the book for 60,000 shares.

- 10,000 at £20.02 = £200,200 (the level is emptied).
- 15,000 at £20.03 = £300,450.
- 20,000 at £20.05 = £401,000.
- 15,000 of the 25,000 at £20.08 = £301,200.

Total £1,202,850, so the average is $1{,}202{,}850 / 60{,}000 = \text{£}20.0475$. At the mid 60,000 shares cost £1,200,000, so the cost is **£2,850**, or 23.75 bp.

**(b) Six slices.** Each 10,000-share order fits in the top level, so it pays £20.02, 2p over the mid. The cost is $60{,}000 \times 0.02 = \text{£}1{,}200$, or 10 bp. This assumes the book refills at the same prices between slices, so the fund's own buying never moves the price.

**(c) Limit bids.** Per share, a fill costs $-2$p and a miss costs $+3$p, so
$$E = 0.6 \times (-2) + 0.4 \times 3 = 0 \text{p}.$$
The expected cost is **£0**. If all six fill the fund earns $60{,}000 \times 0.02 = \text{£}1{,}200$; if none fill it pays $60{,}000 \times 0.03 = \text{£}1{,}800$. The expected value hides a wide range.

**(d) Recommendation.** Never send one 60,000-share market order: it pays more than twice the sliced cost. Post passive bids early in the day, and switch any unfilled shares to market orders or the closing auction before the deadline, since a miss at the end of the day is very costly. In the model $p = 0.6$ is well above the break-even $c/(2h + c) = 1/5$, so passive orders are worth trying while there is time.

**Why it may be too optimistic.** First, adverse selection: bids tend to fill just before the price falls, so fills are worse than they look. Second, market impact: 60,000 shares of buying pushes the price up, so the book does not refill at the same prices, and other traders may spot the pattern and trade ahead.

rubric.text: Walks the book correctly for (a): fills of 10,000, 15,000, 20,000 and 15,000. Finds an average of £20.0475 and a cost of £2,850 against the mid.
Finds £1,200 for the six slices and states the assumption that the book refills at the same prices.
Computes the limit plan's expected cost as $0.6 \times (-2) + 0.4 \times 3 = 0$p a share, or £0.
Gives the range for (c): a gain of £1,200 if all fill, a cost of £1,800 if none do.
Names two reasons the plans are optimistic, such as adverse selection, market impact, the book not refilling, or information leakage.
Recommends a plan that avoids one big market order and handles the deadline, justified by urgency or the break-even $p > c/(2h + c)$.
